statevector.intro: Classifying 2026 as 'an El Niño' says less than it seems. The useful question is how the whole state vector compares to its closest analogues — because 2026 can look like 2015-16 on one variable and like 1997-98 on another, and those two monsters produced opposite Indian monsoons. This is the tracking layer the series has been building toward.

compare.desc: The SST index family for 2026 (current) against the peaks of the two closest strong-El Niño analogues. All three share the same °C scale; SOI, MEI, IOD and monsoon sit in the table below because they run on different units.
compare.inference: The surface is already at 2015-16 intensity — the weekly Niño 3.4 is matched. The smoothed indices (ONI, RONI) sit well below the analogue peaks, but that is a timing gap, not a ceiling: they lag the surface and are climbing fast toward Oct–Dec. Read the shape, not the levels — 2026 is where 2015-16 was months before its peak, with coupling running harder.

statevector.inference: The vector points two ways at once, and that is the finding. On the ocean and coupling, 2026 tracks 2015-16 — a strong El Niño, monsoon-suppressing, India hot and dry. But the decisive difference between the two analogues was the IOD: 1997-98 paired its monster El Niño with a strong positive IOD and India still got a near-normal monsoon, while 2015-16's weak IOD let the deficit through. 2026's IOD is neutral and forecast to turn positive. Which analogue 2026 rhymes with — the 2015-16 deficit or the 1997-98 rescue — is being decided in the Indian Ocean right now, not the Pacific.
